guides.title: Email security guides
guides.subtitle: Understand SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and MTA-STS to protect your domain against email spoofing and phishing.
guides.ctaSubtitle: Test your SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and MTA-STS configuration in one click. Our tool analyzes your domain and tells you exactly what to fix.
guides.spfDescription: SPF defines which servers are authorized to send emails for your domain. It's the first line of defense against email address spoofing.
guides.dkimDescription: DKIM uses asymmetric cryptography to sign your emails. It ensures the content hasn't been modified in transit and that the email actually comes from your domain.
guides.dmarcDescription: DMARC orchestrates SPF and DKIM by defining a clear policy for emails that fail verification. It also adds a reporting system to monitor your domain.
guides.mtaStsTitle: MTA-STS (Mail Transfer Agent Strict Transport Security)
guides.mtaStsDescription: MTA-STS enforces TLS encryption between mail servers, preventing downgrade attacks and email interception in transit.
guides.compDescription: Understand the differences between SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, and how these three protocols work together to protect your domain.

dns.spf_softfail: SPF in softfail (~all) — unauthorized emails are not rejected
dns.spf_neutral: SPF in neutral mode (?all) — no protection
dns.spf_pass_all: SPF with +all — DANGER: allows anyone to send
dns.dmarc_none: DMARC in monitoring mode (p=none) — does not block spoofing
dns.dmarc_quarantine: DMARC in quarantine — spoofed emails go to spam but are not rejected
dns.dmarc_no_reporting: No DMARC reporting configured (rua=) — you won't see spoofing attempts
dns.rec_add_dmarc: Add a DMARC record: _dmarc.yourdomain TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject; adkim=s; aspf=s; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain"
dns.rec_add_dmarc_why: Without DMARC, receiving mail servers have no way to know what to do when SPF or DKIM checks fail. Anyone can send emails pretending to be from your domain, and most servers will deliver them. DMARC with p=reject tells receivers to block unauthorized emails entirely.
dns.rec_dmarc_none_to_reject: Change your DMARC policy from p=none to p=reject to block spoofing
dns.rec_dmarc_none_to_reject_why: With p=none, your DMARC record only monitors — it doesn't actually block spoofed emails. Attackers can still send emails as your domain and they'll be delivered normally. Switching to p=reject instructs receiving servers to drop fraudulent messages before they reach the inbox.
dns.rec_dmarc_quarantine_to_reject: Upgrade your DMARC policy from p=quarantine to p=reject for full blocking
dns.rec_dmarc_quarantine_to_reject_why: With p=quarantine, spoofed emails are sent to spam instead of being blocked outright. Some recipients still check spam folders, and sophisticated attacks can be flagged as legitimate by users. p=reject ensures fraudulent emails never reach any folder.
dns.rec_add_rua: Add rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain to your DMARC to receive reports
dns.rec_add_rua_why: Without DMARC reporting (rua=), you have no visibility into who is sending email on behalf of your domain. Aggregate reports let you detect spoofing attempts, identify misconfigured legitimate senders, and confidently tighten your policy over time.
dns.rec_add_spf: Add an SPF record: yourdomain TXT "v=spf1 include:yourprovider -all"
dns.rec_add_spf_why: SPF tells receiving servers which IP addresses are allowed to send email for your domain. Without it, any server in the world can send emails appearing to come from you. Adding SPF with -all (hardfail) means unauthorized senders will be rejected.
dns.rec_harden_spf: Harden your SPF by replacing ~all with -all (hardfail)
dns.rec_harden_spf_why: With ~all (softfail), unauthorized senders are flagged but emails are usually still delivered. Switching to -all (hardfail) explicitly tells receiving servers to reject emails from unauthorized sources, providing much stronger protection against spoofing.
dns.rec_add_dkim: Enable DKIM in your email provider and add the public key to your DNS zone
dns.rec_add_dkim_why: DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to your emails, proving they haven't been tampered with in transit and genuinely originated from your domain. Without it, attackers can forge emails that pass basic checks, and your legitimate emails are more likely to land in spam.
dns.mta_sts_policy_fetch_error: MTA-STS policy file could not be fetched (https://mta-sts.domain/.well-known/mta-sts.txt)
dns.mta_sts_mode_none: MTA-STS in mode none — TLS is not enforced
dns.mta_sts_mode_testing: MTA-STS in testing mode — failures are reported but mail is still delivered without TLS
dns.rec_add_mta_sts: Add MTA-STS to enforce TLS encryption for incoming emails
dns.rec_add_mta_sts_why: Without MTA-STS, an attacker performing a man-in-the-middle attack can downgrade the connection between mail servers to plaintext, intercepting emails in transit. MTA-STS tells sending servers to only deliver via TLS with a valid certificate, preventing downgrade attacks.
dns.rec_mta_sts_enforce: Switch your MTA-STS policy from testing to enforce mode
dns.rec_mta_sts_enforce_why: In testing mode, MTA-STS only reports TLS failures without blocking delivery. Switching to enforce mode ensures that emails are only delivered over encrypted connections, providing real protection against interception.
dns.rec_fix_mta_sts_policy: Fix your MTA-STS policy file — it could not be fetched
dns.rec_fix_mta_sts_policy_why: Your domain has an MTA-STS DNS record, but the policy file at https://mta-sts.yourdomain/.well-known/mta-sts.txt is unreachable. Without a valid policy file, MTA-STS provides no protection. Check that the subdomain mta-sts.yourdomain resolves correctly and serves the policy over HTTPS.

faq.question: What is email spoofing?
faq.answer: Email spoofing is an identity theft technique where someone sends an email pretending to be someone else. The attacker forges the sender address so the message appears to come from a legitimate source, like your company or a colleague. It's one of the most common methods used in phishing attacks.

faq.question: How do I know if my domain is vulnerable?
faq.answer: Use our free tool: simply enter your domain name in the search bar above. SpoofCheck automatically analyzes your DNS records (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MTA-STS) and tells you if your domain is protected against email spoofing.

faq.question: What are SPF, DKIM, and DMARC?
faq.answer: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) defines which servers are authorized to send emails for your domain. DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) adds a cryptographic signature to your emails to ensure their integrity. DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) combines SPF and DKIM and defines what to do when authentication fails.

faq.question: How do I fix an email vulnerability?
faq.answer: To protect your domain, you need to properly configure three DNS records: an SPF record listing your authorized sending servers, DKIM keys for signing your emails, and a DMARC policy telling receiving servers how to handle unauthenticated emails.

faq.question: Is this test free?
faq.answer: Yes, SpoofCheck is 100% free. You can check as many domains as you want, with no signup or limits. DNS checks are public and non-intrusive.
